# Forensic Dossier — thyssenkrupp AG (TKA.DE)

*Interrogator's report to the Investment Committee · transcripts FY24/25 Q1 (2025-02-13) → FY25/26 Q1 (2026-02-12) · cross-referenced against screener financials and live corrections as of 2026-03-31.*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these six quarters is **not** an operating turnaround — it is a **disassembly**. Management's language migrates steadily away from "we will fix the businesses" and toward "we will break the company into independently listed parts and let the market value them." The through-line is the **ACES 2030 holding-company conversion**.

- **Q1 24/25 (Feb-2025):** The frame is still *operational resilience + portfolio tidying*. The two named portfolio items are a **Marine Systems minority spin** ("finalize in the course of calendar year 2025") and a **Steel Europe 50/50 JV with EPCG**. APEX (cost program) is "2.0," restructuring is "necessary but paves the way." Green-transformation proof-points (CO2 steel for VW, Polysius carbon capture, nucera electrolyzers) are floated as future demand. Net cash is the recurring anchor: "€4.3 billion net cash."
- **Q2 (May-2025):** The Steel narrative hardens — "agreement in principle with IG Metall," AT cost-cut of "€150 million" plus "phaseout of the production site in Hagen." Marine momentum builds (Singapore submarine extension). The group "repaid our last bond… makes the group debt-free."
- **Q3 (Aug-2025):** The pivot is now explicit and structural: thyssenkrupp as "a **strategic holding company with independently managed business segments**… unlock and crystallize value." New CFO Axel Hamann arrives. AT is split "into 4 business units to sharpen our capital market readiness." Steel restructuring agreement "reached consensus this July."
- **Q4 / FY (Dec-2025):** **ACES 2030** is formally branded; "year of decisions" → "**year of execution**." TKMS spin **completed and listed** (Oct-20, MDAX inclusion, "over 14% value creation… on top of the preceding tkAG share price increase of approximately 240%"). Steel pivots from JV to an outright **sale to Jindal** ("majority"). HKM exit agreed with Salzgitter; slab supply to TK Steel "will already end in 2028."
- **Q1 25/26 (Feb-2026):** Materials Services pushed "for capital market readiness and their respective stand-alone setup"; Automation Engineering put up for sale; Jindal due diligence "on its way." The new tailwind introduced: **EU steel policy** (CBAM, safeguard tariffs) — "they do present upside potential."

**Growth drivers quietly dropped:** the green-transformation / hydrogen (nucera) story, front-and-center in 2025, has faded to background — by Q1 25/26 Decarbon Technologies sales are *−19%* with nucera electrolyzer weakness explicitly called out. The thesis has **contracted from "green industrial champion" to "holdco that monetizes hidden assets (TKMS, TKE, Materials) and amputates Steel."**

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Quarter | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|

Net cash fell from ~€5B (Sep-25) to €3.2B (Dec-25) to €2.74B as restructuring cash-out and seasonal NWC bit | **True but eroding.** The balance sheet is the genuine crown jewel and a real SoP add-back, but the cash pile is **shrinking** as restructuring is funded. |

Beat rate only **1 of 6 quarters (17%)** | **Operationally credible on EBIT, weak on delivery.** They defend the profit line via cost-out, but the broader guidance/delivery record is poor (17% beat rate; EPS 3-yr CAGR −25.6%). |

**Net:** the EBIT-resilience claim survives scrutiny; the FCF and "company is healthy" claims do **not**. The real value is **balance-sheet + listed-stub** value (net cash, TKMS, TKE, soon Materials), **not** earnings power.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY — **PIVOTING (defensive on ops, offensive on portfolio)**

- **Q1 24/25:** Cautiously offensive — "record-breaking new orders at Marine," guidance *raised* on FCF. *"Quarter 1 figures look promising to us."*
- **Q2:** More defensive — *"markets don't help… many industries remain muted"*; sales guidance lowered, profit held. LTI accrual hit from the share-price run-up is a tell of how far the stock had already moved.
- **Q3:** New CFO, careful and hedged — EBIT guidance "specified… to the lower end"; net income −€255M with a €150M deferred-tax write-off from the spin mechanics.
- **Q4:** Confident on **portfolio** ("year of execution," TKMS done), guarded on **steel** ("cannot be excluded" re further impairments — said three separate times across Q3/Q4/Q1).
- **Q1 25/26:** Markedly more upbeat on the **external** lever — *"the sentiment has turned… increases in the share prices of around 50%… clear positive sentiment"* on EU steel policy — but this is borrowed confidence from a **sector-wide** re-rating, not company execution.

The shift from offensive (growth/green) to defensive (efficiency/cost/macro-policy) language is unmistakable. Confidence is **rising on the breakup mechanics and falling on the underlying industrial demand.**

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY — **Medium**

They have done what they said on **two things that matter**: (a) delivered three straight years of positive FCF-before-M&A as promised, and (b) executed the TKMS spin on the stated calendar-2025 timetable. That is a real, checkable track record of doing the portfolio things they commit to.

But the **earnings beat rate is 17% (1/6)**, EPS 3-yr CAGR is −25.6%, and "we keep profit guidance" was only achievable by repeatedly **lowering the sales** assumption underneath it. Steel impairments recur every quarter despite "this is hopefully the last one" (said in Q2 and again implied later). The guidance is **directionally honest but consistently set at a level the top line keeps undercutting** — credible on portfolio milestones, soft on operating delivery. **Reliability: Medium.**

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts (Synagowitz of Deutsche Bank, Fairclough, Obst, Gabriel) circle the **same four unanswered questions** call after call:

1. **"Net cash €4B+, market cap €3B — you could buy the whole company back"** (Fairclough, Q1 24/25). Lopez deflects: *"We are not doing this theoretical analysis right now."* The SoP discount is so glaring that analysts state it to management's face; management refuses to engage.
2. **How much cash gets trapped/seeded into each spun entity?** Repeatedly pushed (Synagowitz Q3: "is there a floor you could guide us towards"). Management **will not disclose** the starting balance sheet of the spun businesses — a recurring non-answer that matters enormously for the residual TKA stub value.
3. **Marine guarantees / freed capital** (Fairclough Q1): management concedes the guarantees "**do not immediately free up capital**" — puncturing a bull talking point.
4. **Further Steel impairments?** Asked every quarter; answer is always "cannot be excluded." This is the topic that has **repeatedly turned into bad news** (the €600M FY25 steel impairment).

What analysts worry about that management isn't addressing: **the residual stub.** As TKMS, then Materials, then potentially TKE and Steel leave, what is left in TKA AG, what net cash stays vs. seeds the spins, and what the holding-company conglomerate discount on the remaining pieces will be.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Steel is a serial value-destroyer** — €600M+ of FY25's €800M impairments; ROIC −2%, "cannot be excluded" re further write-downs (Q1 25/26).
🔴 **TTM FCF is −€926M** (live) despite the "3 years positive FCF" headline — the cash story depends on Marine prepayments and a before-M&A definition.
🔴 **Net cash is melting** — €5B (Sep-25) → €3.2B (Dec-25) → €2.74B (Mar-26) as restructuring (€700–800M guided FY25/26) is funded out of the balance sheet.
🔴 **Revenue in secular decline** — −6% to −8% YoY every quarter; the conglomerate is shrinking, not stabilizing.
🔴 **Steel slab self-supply ends 2028** (HKM exit) — a structural input-cost cliff for the steel stub.
🔴 **17% earnings beat rate** and EPS 3-yr CAGR −25.6%.

🟢 **TKMS spin executed and value-accretive** — completed Oct-2025, MDAX, "14% value creation"; the retained 51% ≈ €2.7B is real, listed, mark-to-market value.
🟢 **Genuine net-cash balance sheet** (€2.74B) and **group is bond-debt-free** — a real SoP add-back, rare for a distressed industrial.
🟢 **Materials Services / tk accelis is the next dated crystallization** — capital-market-readiness push; a clean, profitable (€11.4B sales, €50M+ EBIT-adj/qtr) trading franchise.
🟢 **EBIT-adjusted held flat through a €2.2B revenue drop** — cost discipline (APEX) is real; 4,800 FTE out in FY25.
🟢 **TKE (Elevator) stake** booked ~€2B with optionality ("talk in the market around IPO").

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **Terminology migration:** "portfolio optimization" (early) → "**strategic holding company**" (Q3) → "**lean financial holding company**" / "ACES 2030" (Q4–Q1 25/26). The endpoint became explicit only late: TKA wants to be a **financial holding** owning stakes, not an operator. That reframes the correct valuation lens from earnings to **sum-of-the-stubs minus stub holdco discount**.
- **The Steel exit route flipped** — from "50/50 JV with EPCG" (Q1 24/25) to "sale to Jindal, majority" (Q4). [POST-TRANSCRIPT: this has since flipped *again* — see §8 / catalyst verification.] The instability of the Steel disposal path across four quarters is itself a credibility signal: they do not control this outcome.
- **New CFO Hamann** is more numerate and more hedged than predecessor Schulte — more willing to say "cannot be excluded," "too early to tell," "we won't provide further detail." Less salesmanship, more risk-flagging.
- **Capital allocation is conspicuously NOT a buyback** despite analysts repeatedly pointing out the company trades below net cash + stakes. Management's refusal ("not within the next 24 months") signals cash is **earmarked for restructuring and spin-seeding**, not shareholder returns — confirming the stub-dilution worry.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is a **special-situation breakup / holdco-conversion**, not an operating turnaround. The correct way to underwrite TKA is sum-of-parts (net cash + TKMS 51% + TKE stake + Materials/tk accelis + a near-zero-or-negative option on Steel), **minus** the cash that seeds each spin and the residual-stub conglomerate discount — **not** a P/E or P/FCF on the consolidated entity (where TTM FCF is negative and ROIC is −2%).

**The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing:** *how much of the visible asset value actually accrues to the TKA stub vs. leaks away.* Every spin is a **minority (49%) distribution** that hands value directly to existing TKA holders (good) but also **consolidates a shrinking, cash-seeded residual** at the parent. The net-cash crown jewel is **melting** (€5B→€2.74B in two quarters) into restructuring. And the one catalyst that would have crystallized the worst asset — the **Jindal Steel sale** — is exactly the kind of serially-reshaped, third-party-dependent process that has flipped twice and may not close. Underwrite the **parts you can mark today** (net cash, listed TKMS, TKE) and treat Steel and any not-yet-fired spin as **option value, not base value.**

**ECONOMIC MOAT:** **NONE / ERODING.** thyssenkrupp's consolidated returns are negative (ROIC −2.0%, ROE −4.1%), gross margin 11.3% is thin for a capital-goods+steel mix, and the moat is whatever **scale-cost** advantage the individual franchises (Materials trading, TKMS submarines) carry — *not* the conglomerate. The submarine business (TKMS) genuinely has a **regulatory-license / sovereign-customer** moat, but it has already been spun out and is no longer the value driver inside TKA's *operating* base. The steel business has **no moat** — it is a structurally disadvantaged, sub-scale, high-cost European integrated producer that earns below its cost of capital and is being given away.

**SECULAR THREAT — material (not terminal for the holdco):** European integrated steel faces **energy-transition / decarbonization cost displacement** (green-steel capex with no return, carbon costs, Chinese/Asian overcapacity) — a structural impairment to the *Steel* stub's terminal value. *But* the holding-company value is dominated by **non-steel** parts (net cash, defense, elevators, materials trading) that do **not** share that tail. So the secular force is **material to one amputated limb, manageable at the holdco level.** The cheapness here is **NOT** a melting-base value trap *if* you underwrite the stubs and assign Steel ~zero; it **becomes** a value trap if you credit a consolidated earnings recovery (which the financials do not support).

# Forensic Dossier — thyssenkrupp AG (TKA.DE)

*Industrials · diversified industrial holding (steel, automotive technology, materials trading, decarbon/hydrogen tech, 51% of marine/TKMS, ~16% TK Elevator) · signal_type: deep_value · transcripts Q1 FY24/25 (2025-02) → Q1 FY25/26 (2026-02)*

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these six quarters is a **conglomerate self-liquidation narrative dressed as a "green transformation,"** and the emphasis migrates decisively over the window. Early calls (Feb 2025) lead with operations — APEX 2.0 cost program, "resilience," a record Marine order backlog (€16bn), CO2-reduced steel MOUs with Volkswagen, electrolyzer MOUs. By the Dec-2025 full-year call the lead has become explicitly **portfolio-and-structure**: management unveils "ACES 2030," reframes the entire company as a future "**financial holding company with strong independent entities**," and stops pretending the operating businesses are the thesis. The throughline is *value crystallization through separation*, with TKMS the proof-of-concept.

What got **introduced**: the holding-company end-state (Dec-2025), the Jindal majority-sale track for Steel (Dec-2025), the Materials Services "capital market readiness" track (Feb-2026), the Automotive realignment into 4 BUs + divestment of Automation Engineering (Aug-2025→Feb-2026), the HKM exit / Salzgitter term sheet ending captive slab supply in 2028 (Feb-2026). What got **executed**: the TKMS minority spin-off (49% distributed, 51% retained, 1:20 ratio, listed Frankfurt Oct-2025, into MDAX within weeks) — management claims "over 14% value creation … on the first day" on top of a "~240% [TK] share price increase in fiscal year '24-'25."

The growth-driver that was loudly introduced and is being **quietly dropped** is the green-hydrogen story. Decarbon Technologies (nucera electrolyzers, Polysius cement-capture, Uhde ammonia) is presented every quarter as "the future," yet by Feb-2026 it is the *worst* segment — sales −19%, EBIT −€33m to −€16m on "project deferrals." The MOUs (VW, TITAN, Hydrom, Uniper) are non-binding framework agreements that recur as talking points without converting to revenue. The real, repeating *good news* is narrow and concentrated: Marine Systems (now spun) and Bilstein aftermarket. Everything else is "weak demand across most customer groups."

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Quarter(s) | The hard numbers say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Increasing underlying resilience … EBIT adjusted stable despite ~€5bn sales drop in 2 years" | repeated, esp. Dec-25 | Revenue 41.1B (FY22) → 37.5B → 35.0B → **32.8B (FY25)**, 3-yr CAGR **−7.2%**. EBIT-adj did hold ~€640m FY25 (+€72m YoY). | **Half-true.** Adjusted EBIT genuinely defended via FTE cuts (−4,800 FY25), but it sits atop a revenue base shrinking 6-7%/yr. Defending a margin on a melting top line is not resilience, it is managed decline. |

Q1 FY25/26 alone was −€1.5bn. |

Q1 FY25/26 NI **−€334m**. ROE −4.1%, ROIC −2.0%. | **Manufactured.** The single positive year is a valuation/disposal artifact, not operating earnings. Underlying remains loss-making; returns are *below zero*. |

The decisive forensic point: **every positive headline number in the window traces to a one-off** (Marine prepayment → FCF; Elevator revaluation + India sale → net income; disposals → net cash). The *recurring* operating engine produces negative ROIC, −6-7% revenue, and 1.4% net margin.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-rising on STRATEGY, persistently defensive on OPERATIONS** — a widening split between confident portfolio language and apologetic demand language.

- **Feb-2025** (Lopez/Schulte): offensive on Marine ("record breaking new orders," "my personal highlight"), measured on markets ("many industries remain muted … automotive under pressure"). Schulte volunteers the famous tell on the call's last exchange — analyst Fairclough: *"your net cash is over €4 billion. Your market cap is €3 billion … you could just buy the whole company back, right?"* Lopez deflects: *"We are not doing this theoretical analysis right now."*
- **May-2025**: more defensive — *"markets remain weak overall,"* AT cost-cut of €150m + Hagen phase-out, *"down by 2,600 FTE."* The LTI-accrual confession (>€30m hit *because* the share price ran) is candid.
- **Aug-2025** (new CFO Hamann debuts): hedged — guidance "specified … to the lower end," sales −9% in the quarter. Repeated *"cannot be excluded"* on further Steel impairments.
- **Dec-2025**: most confident of the window, but the confidence is entirely **structural** — "year of decisions," "year of execution," ACES 2030, TKMS "blueprint," "over 14% value creation." Operations still "persistent market headwinds."
- **Feb-2026**: a genuinely new, *more bullish* note appears — Steel sentiment "turned positive … share prices up ~50%," CBAM/tariff "upside potential," ETS-delay "another de-risking factor," Steel Summit with Chancellor Merz / von der Leyen. This is the first quarter management talks *up* an operating business (steel) on exogenous policy tailwinds rather than purely on self-help.

The shift from offensive→defensive→structural-offensive is the signature of a **break-up story finding traction**: confidence is highest where the lever is corporate-finance (separation), lowest where it is end-market demand.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: MEDIUM.** The screener's earnings-beat rate is brutal — **1 of 6 quarters (17%)**, EPS 3-yr CAGR −25.6% — and on the *operating* line the pattern is serial top-line guide-downs ("lowered our sales guidance" Q1; "specified to the lower end" Q3). So on demand/EPS, credibility is LOW and the numbers confirm it.

BUT the credibility *splits by metric*: on **FCF-before-M&A** management hit its guide three years running (even raising it once) and on **portfolio milestones** they delivered the headline acts — TKMS spun on schedule (Oct-2025), India electrical-steel sold (~€440m, closed Jan-2025), IG Metall restructuring agreed (Dec-2025), the bond repaid (debt-free). They **deliver on transactions and cash-timing; they miss on operating demand.** No sandbagging pattern — if anything the FCF guide is *honestly* flagged as one-off-flattered ("we did not simply add the €1bn"). Score the *deal-execution* track HIGH, the *operating-guidance* track LOW; blended MEDIUM.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts (Synagowitz/Bastian most persistently, Fairclough, Obst, Gabriel) circle four unanswered things, and management deflects each:

1. **How much cash gets trapped/injected into the Steel carve-out?** Asked Aug-2025 ("is there a floor?") and answered with *"it will have the required liquidity"* — no number, repeatedly. This is the load-bearing unknown for the SoP and they will not quantify it.
2. **Marine prepayment magnitude / what's really in the cash balance.** Schulte (Feb-25): *"we would not disclose any further figures … it's above €1 billion."* The net-cash number is partly customer money.
3. **Restructuring cash-out cadence.** Guided €250m FY25 + 3-digit-€m FY26 Steel + undefined Auto; Feb-26 escalated to **€700-800m total restructuring**. The cash drag keeps getting *bigger* each time they're pushed.
4. **Will further Steel impairments come?** Every quarter: *"cannot be excluded."* They never get to "no."

The topic analysts pushed that *later turned into news*: the **Steel sale structure** — Synagowitz repeatedly probed (Aug-25) whether a better policy backdrop could make TK *retain* steel; Lopez denied ("I would not see any reason right now"). Four months later (Feb-26) management themselves concede the "positive sentiment … will have to be an input for the conversations with Jindal" — i.e., the analyst's hypothesis (policy changes the steel calculus) was right, and it ultimately killed the Jindal deal (see §6).

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **TTM FCF is −€926m** despite the "3 years positive FCF" headline — the positive prints are advance-payment timing, not durable cash generation.
🔴 **Every positive FY25 metric is a one-off** (Elevator revaluation, India sale, Marine prepayment) washing recurring impairments and operating losses; ROE −4.1%, ROIC −2.0%.
🔴 **Revenue in structural decline** (−6 to −7%/yr, three years running) — "resilience" = defending margin while the base shrinks.

🟢 **Transaction-delivery credibility is high** — TKMS spun on time, India sold, bond repaid, restructuring agreed. The break-up machine works.
🟢 **Genuine net-cash balance sheet** (€3.0bn at 2026-03-31, cash €3.84bn > total debt €0.81bn) — a legitimate SoP add-back and downside cushion.
🟢 **EU steel policy tailwind is a new, exogenous positive** (CBAM tightening, import quotas, ETS-delay) that re-rated European steel ~50% in 4 months and ultimately let TK keep Steel on better terms.

Hamann is notably more transactional/finance-holding in framing — he is the voice of "tk accelis," "capital market readiness," "MaaS," the deferred-tax-asset write-down mechanics. The new CFO is a *break-up CFO*, signalling the holding-company pivot is structural, not rhetorical.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING** — decisively, and competently, from operating-industrial to financial-holding/serial-separator. This is a genuine self-help break-up executed by a credible deal team, not a drift.

# thyssenkrupp AG (TKA.DE) — Forensic Dossier

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from six consecutive quarterly calls (February 2025 through February 2026) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials. thyssenkrupp is a sprawling German industrial conglomerate — steel, auto parts, materials trading, plant engineering, submarines and a leftover elevator stake — in the middle of breaking itself apart into a "financial holding company." The whole story here is about that break-up, not about the operating business, which is shrinking.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story management tells has shifted decisively over the last year, from "fix the operations" to "dismantle the conglomerate and crystallize value." In the first quarter call (February 2025) the emphasis was on a single planned move — a minority spin-off of the submarine business, Marine Systems — plus a slow-grinding cost program management calls APEX (its internal efficiency drive). By the third-quarter call (August 2025) the language had hardened into a full corporate doctrine: "shaping the future of thyssenkrupp as a strategic holding company with independently managed business segments… Ultimately, our goal is to unlock and crystallize value for our shareholders." By the full-year call (December 2025) this had a name — "ACES 2030" — and a completed proof point: the Marine Systems spin-off (now listed as TKMS) was done, with management claiming "over 14% value creation… on top of the preceding [thyssenkrupp] share price increase of approximately 240% in fiscal year '24-'25."

The growth drivers introduced and quietly re-weighted along the way tell the real story. Early on, three threads ran in parallel: the submarine spin, a 50/50 steel joint venture with the Czech investor EPCG, and "green transformation" wins (hydrogen, carbon capture, low-carbon steel). Over the year the EPCG steel JV quietly mutated into a *sale* of the steel division to India's Jindal (first surfaced December 2025), the green-transformation talk faded from a headline driver to a recurring footnote of memorandums and awards, and a new front opened: making Materials Services (the metals-trading arm) "capital-market ready" for its own listing. The narrative, in short, expanded from one spin to a serial break-up — and the load-bearing asset shifted from submarines (done) to steel (now in flux) to the elevator stake and Materials Services (still ahead).

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

The operating business is in clear secular and cyclical decline; management's claims are almost entirely about *self-help and portfolio actions*, not organic recovery — and on that narrow ground, the numbers broadly corroborate them.

| Management claim | The actual financials | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Most KPIs above the prior year… solid quarter" (Q1 FY25) | Revenue down 6.3% year over year, with a three-year revenue decline of about 7% a year; sales fell roughly €5B over two years | Story is richer than the top line — true only at the earnings/cash line, not revenue |
| "EBIT adjusted stable… increased €72M to €640M" despite falling sales (FY25) | Net margin a thin 1.4%; return on equity −4.1%, return on invested capital −2.0% — the company destroys capital even as adjusted EBIT "rises" | The "adjusted" figure hides ongoing impairments and capital destruction |
| "Third consecutive year of positive free cash flow before M&A… €363M" (FY25) | Trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is *negative* €926M as of March 2026; the annual figure leans on a Marine Systems customer prepayment and is struck "before M&A" and after €250M of restructuring cash-out | The headline cash claim is real but heavily flattered by timing and definition |
| "Strong balance sheet, ~€4-5B net cash" (every call) | Independently recomputed net cash of about €3.03B at March 2026 (cash €3.84B vs total debt €806M) — genuinely net-cash, but down from the €4.3-5B peaks management quoted, and Q1 burned it to €3.2B | Corroborated in direction, but the cash is eroding and seasonally volatile |
| Restructuring "paving the way for future profitability" | Repeated, escalating impairments at Steel (~€600M in FY25 alone) and guidance for €700-800M of restructuring costs in FY26 | The "paving" is expensive and ongoing; profitability is promised, not delivered |

The honest read: every quarter pairs a falling top line with a flat-to-up "adjusted" earnings line and a cash number propped by one-offs. Earnings per share swung from −€3.33 (FY23) to −€2.42 (FY24) to a thin +€0.75 (FY25), and the latest quarter's earnings per share is essentially zero (+€0.01 trailing twelve months). This is a company whose *reported* recovery is almost entirely a restructuring-and-portfolio artifact, not a demand recovery.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-rising on portfolio confidence, but persistently defensive on the operating business.** Management's voice is consistent and disciplined, never euphoric. The dominant register is defensive: "markets don't help at the moment" (Q1 FY25), "markets remain weak overall" (Q2), "weak demand as well as some overwhelming macro uncertainties" (Q3), "a difficult market environment persists" (Q1 FY26). Against that, the *portfolio* language grows steadily more confident and concrete — from "we want to finalize in the course of calendar year 2025" (Q1 FY25) to "we are fully on track for the listing" (Q3) to "we have completed the spin-off, unlocking significant value" (FY25). The clearest tell is the new Steel optimism in the February 2026 call: "the sentiment has turned into a positive one for the last 4 months… increases in the share prices of around 50%," and references to direct talks with Chancellor Merz and EU Commission President von der Leyen on steel tariffs. Confidence is migrating from "we can cut our way through" toward "policy and a higher steel multiple may rescue the asset we were about to sell."

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: Medium.** On the metric they care most about — free cash flow before mergers and acquisitions — management has delivered three years running and even nudged guidance up mid-year (Q1 FY25) on a Marine prepayment, ultimately beating slightly (FY25 came in "slightly better" than the updated guide). They were also candid about the mechanics that flatter it (sales-tax payback, synchronized cash-outs, seasonality). That is a creditable track record on their chosen yardstick. But two things cap the score. First, the screener shows management beat earnings expectations in only 1 of the last 6 quarters (a 17% rate) — the *earnings* line is unreliable, repeatedly torpedoed by impairments management always frames as "hopefully the last one" and then books again. Second, they serially lowered the *sales* guide every quarter while holding the profit guide, a sandbag-and-shuffle pattern: cut the top line, defend the bottom line with cost actions. Credible on cash, evasive-by-omission on the recurring impairment drumbeat.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts circled the same three soft spots all year, and management deflected each:
- **"You could just buy the whole company back" (Jason Fairclough, Q1 FY25):** with net cash then above €4B against a ~€3B market cap, an analyst openly flagged the absurdity. Management refused to engage — "We are not doing this theoretical analysis right now" — and the gap has since closed the wrong way for late buyers (the stock roughly doubled, so this specific arbitrage is now spent).
- **The steel separation's starting balance sheet and cash injection (Bastian Synagowitz, repeatedly):** how much cash must be put *into* steel to hive it off, and what pension and restructuring liabilities travel with it. Management never quantified it — "it will have the required liquidity" — and pensions allocated to Steel were later admitted at about €2.4B, a large hidden liability against any sale price.
- **Trapped capital in Marine guarantees (Jason Fairclough, Q1 FY25):** the hoped-for "freeing up capital" was walked back — "it does not immediately free up capital." A bull talking point was quietly defused by management itself.

The topic analysts pushed that *did* turn into news: the steel sale. Pushed all year on whether they might retain steel given improving policy, management insisted on selling the majority to Jindal — and then, after this transcript window, those talks were paused (see the verdict section).

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Recurring, large, "final" impairments at Steel that are never actually final — about €600M in FY25, guided €700-800M of restructuring in FY26.
🔴 Pension and restructuring liabilities (~€2.4B pensions at Steel alone) that materially shrink the net cash that bulls anchor on.
🔴 The operating business is genuinely shrinking — revenue down three years straight, returns on capital negative — so the thesis rests entirely on financial engineering, not a turnaround.
🔴 Free cash flow flattered by customer prepayments and "before M&A / before restructuring" definitions; trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is actually negative.
🔴 CFO turnover mid-saga (Jens Schulte handed to Axel Hamann around the Q3 FY25 call) during the most complex portfolio work.

🟢 Genuinely net-cash (~€3.0B) and effectively debt-free after repaying its last bond — rare for a distressed-looking industrial.
🟢 A real, *completed* value-crystallization (the TKMS submarine spin, October 2025) — proof the holding-company plan can execute, not just slideware.
🟢 Visible, sustained headcount reduction (4,800 in FY25) that is actually flowing into adjusted EBIT despite falling sales.
🟢 Marine Systems is a structural winner riding European defense spending, with a record order backlog above €16B.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The vocabulary migration is the signal. "Minority spin" (Q1) became "stand-alone businesses… open to third parties" and "financial holding company" (FY25) — the ambition widened from one carve-out to dismantling the whole group. Steel's framing flipped twice: from a "50/50 JV with EPCG," to a *sale* to Jindal, to (in February 2026) a coy openness to "crystallize the value of the steel unit in a different way" as European steel multiples re-rated ~50% on tariff hopes. Watch also the renaming of Materials Services to "tk accelis" and the "KGaA" structure chatter — a German corporate form that lets the parent keep control while selling a majority economic stake, signalling management wants the value *and* the control. Finally, the elevator (TK Elevator) stake — booked at around €2B — keeps surfacing in analyst questions as the next hidden asset to monetize, with IPO talk swirling; management stays deliberately noncommittal ("we're super happy with our share").

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is not an operating turnaround; it is a deliberate, partly-executed self-liquidation of a conglomerate into separately-valued parts, run by a credible-on-cash, defensive-on-demand management team. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the load-bearing catalysts are now mostly spent or in flux** — the submarine spin already happened (the re-rating it drove is behind us, and the stock has already roughly doubled), and the steel sale to Jindal that anchored the break-up has, after this transcript window, been paused. What's left (the Materials Services / "tk accelis" 49% spin, with an extraordinary shareholder vote scheduled, and the elevator-stake monetization) is real and dated, but partly priced, against an operating base that is shrinking with negative returns on capital and ~€2.4B of steel pensions that eat into the cash cushion.

**Moat:** none in the durable sense. Steel and metals-distribution are commodity, scale-cost businesses with no pricing power (gross margin ~11%, returns on capital negative); the one genuinely advantaged unit, submarines, has already been spun out to 51%. **Moat type:** scale-cost in steel (cyclical, not durable) and a regulatory-license/defense moat in marine (now mostly outside the parent). **Moat trend:** eroding at the group level — adjusted EBIT is being defended by cost cuts, not by pricing or share gains.

**Secular threat:** material, not terminal. The clearest structural tail is energy-transition pressure on legacy steel and internal-combustion auto components (the green-steel pivot is precisely an attempt to outrun it), but European steel is currently being *protected* by tariffs and import quotas — a policy tailwind that offsets the secular headwind for now. The cheapness is therefore best read as a fear-print on a shrinking, capital-destroying base partly *backstopped* by a large pile of crystallizable assets — closer to a special-situation break-up play than either a clean value bargain or a pure value trap. Size it as a sum-of-the-parts/break-up bet, not as a quality compounder, and only after the easy re-rating has already happened.

The operating business is in clear secular and cyclical decline; management's claims are almost entirely about *self-help and portfolio actions*, not organic recovery — and on that narrow ground, the numbers broadly corroborate them.

**Reliability: Medium.** On the metric they care most about — free cash flow before mergers and acquisitions — management has delivered three years running and even nudged guidance up mid-year (Q1 FY25) on a Marine prepayment, ultimately beating slightly (FY25 came in "slightly better" than the updated guide). ## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Recurring, large, "final" impairments at Steel that are never actually final — about €600M in FY25, guided €700-800M of restructuring in FY26.
🔴 Pension and restructuring liabilities (~€2.4B pensions at Steel alone) that materially shrink the net cash that bulls anchor on.
🔴 The operating business is genuinely shrinking — revenue down three years straight, returns on capital negative — so the thesis rests entirely on financial engineering, not a turnaround.
🔴 Free cash flow flattered by customer prepayments and "before M&A / before restructuring" definitions; trailing-twelve-month free cash flow is actually negative.
🔴 CFO turnover mid-saga (Jens Schulte handed to Axel Hamann around the Q3 FY25 call) during the most complex portfolio work.

🟢 Genuinely net-cash (~€3.0B) and effectively debt-free after repaying its last bond — rare for a distressed-looking industrial.
🟢 A real, *completed* value-crystallization (the TKMS submarine spin, October 2025) — proof the holding-company plan can execute, not just slideware.
🟢 Visible, sustained headcount reduction (4,800 in FY25) that is actually flowing into adjusted EBIT despite falling sales.
🟢 Marine Systems is a structural winner riding European defense spending, with a record order backlog above €16B.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The vocabulary migration is the signal. "Minority spin" (Q1) became "stand-alone businesses… open to third parties" and "financial holding company" (FY25) — the ambition widened from one carve-out to dismantling the whole group. Steel's framing flipped twice: from a "50/50 JV with EPCG," to a *sale* to Jindal, to (in February 2026) a coy openness to "crystallize the value of the steel unit in a different way" as European steel multiples re-rated ~50% on tariff hopes. Watch also the renaming of Materials Services to "tk accelis" and the "KGaA" structure chatter — a German corporate form that lets the parent keep control while selling a majority economic stake, signalling management wants the value *and* the control. Finally, the elevator (TK Elevator) stake — booked at around €2B — keeps surfacing in analyst questions as the next hidden asset to monetize, with IPO talk swirling; management stays deliberately noncommittal ("we're super happy with our share").

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is not an operating turnaround; it is a deliberate, partly-executed self-liquidation of a conglomerate into separately-valued parts, run by a credible-on-cash, defensive-on-demand management team. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the load-bearing catalysts are now mostly spent or in flux** — the submarine spin already happened (the re-rating it drove is behind us, and the stock has already roughly doubled), and the steel sale to Jindal that anchored the break-up has, after this transcript window, been paused. What's left (the Materials Services / "tk accelis" 49% spin, with an extraordinary shareholder vote scheduled, and the elevator-stake monetization) is real and dated, but partly priced, against an operating base that is shrinking with negative returns on capital and ~€2.4B of steel pensions that eat into the cash cushion.

**Moat:** none in the durable sense. Steel and metals-distribution are commodity, scale-cost businesses with no pricing power (gross margin ~11%, returns on capital negative); the one genuinely advantaged unit, submarines, has already been spun out to 51%. **Moat type:** scale-cost in steel (cyclical, not durable) and a regulatory-license/defense moat in marine (now mostly outside the parent). **Moat trend:** eroding at the group level — adjusted EBIT is being defended by cost cuts, not by pricing or share gains.

**Secular threat:** material, not terminal. The clearest structural tail is energy-transition pressure on legacy steel and internal-combustion auto components (the green-steel pivot is precisely an attempt to outrun it), but European steel is currently being *protected* by tariffs and import quotas — a policy tailwind that offsets the secular headwind for now. The cheapness is therefore best read as a fear-print on a shrinking, capital-destroying base partly *backstopped* by a large pile of crystallizable assets — closer to a special-situation break-up play than either a clean value bargain or a pure value trap. Size it as a sum-of-the-parts/break-up bet, not as a quality compounder, and only after the easy re-rating has already happened.

# thyssenkrupp AG (TKA.DE) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator pass. Six consecutive quarterly calls, February 2025 through February 2026, cross-referenced against the screener financials. thyssenkrupp is a German industrial conglomerate breaking itself into pieces: it is turning from an operating group into a "financial holding company" that owns separately-listed businesses. Prices in euros; the shares trade on Xetra (ticker TKA).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these six calls is a single, disciplined message repeated until it came true: **"we will break ourselves up, one piece at a time, and let the market pay for each piece separately."** Management calls the framework ACES 2030 and the destination a "lean financial holding company."

At the start of the window (Q1 FY24-25, February 2025) the emphasis was on a *minority* spin-off of the naval-defense business, Marine Systems (TKMS), during calendar 2025, plus a 50/50 steel joint venture with the Czech energy group EPCG. By the middle of the window the steel plan had mutated — first into a collective restructuring agreement with the IG Metall union (May–July 2025), then into a full **sale** of Steel Europe to India's Jindal Steel (disclosed December 2025). By the end of the window (Q1 FY25-26, February 2026) the holding-company vision had hardened into a queue: Marine Systems already spun and listed; Materials Services being "prepared for capital-market readiness"; Automotive Technology re-cut into four units with a non-core piece (Automation Engineering) put up for sale; Steel in due diligence with Jindal.

The one growth driver that was *introduced and amplified* is defense. Marine Systems moved from a footnote to the centerpiece, riding record submarine orders (Germany, Singapore) to a >€16B backlog. The drivers *quietly dropped* were the green-transformation showcases — hydrogen (nucera), carbon capture (Polysius), green steel — which opened most calls in 2025 as proof points and by early 2026 had faded to boilerplate as their end-markets ("hesitant," "project deferrals") disappointed.

**The marquee promise was kept exactly.** Management said it would spin Marine Systems in calendar 2025 at a 1-for-20 ratio, keeping 51% — and on 20 October 2025 it did precisely that, with the stub added to the MDAX mid-cap index within weeks. In a file full of missed top-line forecasts, that delivered promise is the single most important credibility anchor here.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Increasing underlying resilience… EBIT adjusted up despite sales down" (every call) | FY24-25 EBIT adjusted €640M, up €72M year-over-year, on revenue down ~6% to €32.84B. Net income swung positive to €465M (EPS €0.75) from a €1.51B loss. | **True but fragile.** The EBIT-adjusted line genuinely held while sales fell ~€5B over two years. But "adjusted" does heavy lifting — the reported turn to profit leaned on one-offs (an Elevator-stake revaluation of ~€900M in Q4, the Electrical Steel India sale), offset by ~€800M of Steel impairments. |
| "Third consecutive year of positive free cash flow — first time in 20 years" | FY24-25 free cash flow before M&A €363M — but flattered by a >€1B Marine Systems customer prepayment. TTM free cash flow (to 31 March 2026) is **negative €926M**, and FY25-26 is guided **negative** on €700–800M of restructuring cash-out. | **Poorer than the headline.** The streak is real but thin and prepayment-aided; underlying cash generation has already rolled back over. |
| "Impairments at Steel will stop once the new business plan is agreed" (Feb 2025) | Steel impairments recurred every subsequent quarter — ~€100M (Q2), ~€100M (Q3), ~€600M of the ~€800M full-year total (Q4), and further Steel restructuring charges drove a **−€334M** net loss in Q1 FY25-26. Management now says more "cannot be excluded." | **Did not hold up.** This is the clearest broken promise in the file. |
| "Strong balance sheet, net cash ~€4–5B" | Net cash fell from ~€4.3B (Dec 2024) to €3.7B (Jun 2025), rose to ~€5B at fiscal year-end (Sept 2025) on the India sale, then dropped to €3.2B (Dec 2025) and ~€2.7B (Mar 2026) as cash burned. | **True but eroding.** The cash cushion is real, but it is a melting asset while the operating businesses consume cash and restructuring bills come due. Note it also ignores a large pension deficit (~€2.4B in Steel alone). |
| "We keep profit guidance" (repeatedly) | FY24-25 landed inside the (twice-lowered) EBIT-adjusted range of €600M–€1B at €640M; sales guidance was cut three times across the window. | **Half-credible.** Profit guidance was defended and met; the top-line guide was serially walked down. |

The pattern: the *portfolio* claims are trustworthy (they spun Marine Systems on the letter of the plan), the *profit-resilience* claim is real but adjustment-heavy, and the *cash and impairment* claims have consistently flattered a weaker reality.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-rising on portfolio, defensive on operations.** The confidence is bifurcated. On the breakup, management grew *more* specific and assured over time — from "we want to finalize in the course of calendar 2025" (Feb 2025) to a delivered listing and a concrete queue of next names (Feb 2026). On the underlying business, the language stayed relentlessly defensive: "markets don't help," "many industries remain muted," "weak customer demand, particularly in Europe," repeated call after call, with the offense always framed as self-help (restructuring, headcount out, APEX cost program) rather than growth.

A telling late-window shift: by February 2026 management leaned into *external* tailwinds it does not control — a "positive sentiment" in European steel (share prices "up around 50%"), EU import quotas and CBAM (the carbon border tariff), a possible delay to the EU emissions-trading phase-out. That is a subtle move from "we will fix this ourselves" to "the policy environment may rescue the steel unit" — more hopeful, less controllable.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: Medium.** The screener shows a beat rate of just **1 of 6 quarters (17%)** — chronic under-delivery against consensus — and a three-year EPS CAGR of **−25.6%**. Yet management met its own (lowered) EBIT-adjusted guide for FY24-25 and delivered the Marine Systems spin on schedule and to specification. The reconciliation: they sandbag and re-cut the *sales* line, defend the *adjusted-profit* line, and execute *portfolio* milestones on time. What you cannot trust is any forward statement about impairments ("they will stop") or clean cash flow; what you can trust is a dated, structural portfolio commitment once it is formally announced.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts circled the same three sore spots for a year, and management deflected each:
- **How much cash must be injected to separate Steel?** Asked repeatedly (Synagowitz, Q3); answered only with "it will have the required liquidity" and "not ready by year-end." Still unquantified.
- **The net-cash-versus-market-cap gap.** In February 2025, with net cash over €4B against a ~€3B market cap, an analyst put it bluntly: "you could just buy the whole company back." Management declined the "theoretical analysis." The market has since closed much of that gap, so the pointed version of the question has expired.
- **What frees up when the government backs Marine Systems?** Management conceded the guarantees "don't have to be backed up by cash" and would not put a euro figure on the financing capacity unlocked.

The pattern that later turned into bad news: every time management said Steel impairments would end, analysts pushed, and the impairments kept coming.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🟢 **Delivered the marquee spin exactly as promised** (TKMS, 20 October 2025, 1-for-20, 51/49, MDAX inclusion) — the strongest single credibility mark in the file.
🟢 **Real, verifiable cost-out:** headcount down ~4,800 in FY24-25, EBIT-adjusted defended while revenue fell ~€5B over two years.
🟢 **Genuine hidden assets crystallizing:** a 16.2% TK Elevator stake, booked ~€2B, now subject to a Kone takeover; separately-listed nucera and Marine Systems stakes.
🔴 **The "last impairment" that never is** — Steel impairments recurred every quarter after being declared over.
🔴 **Cash generation has rolled back over** — TTM free cash flow −€926M; FY25-26 guided negative; net cash down from ~€5B to ~€2.7B in six months.
🔴 **Deep operational weakness** — ROIC −2%, ROE −4.1%, net margin 1.4%, revenue −6% year-over-year, Altman-Z 1.8 (a distress-zone reading); the core is a low-return cyclical.
🔴 **The thesis increasingly leans on policy it does not control** (EU steel tariffs, CBAM, ETS delay).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The CFO turnover is worth noting: Jens Schulte handed off to **Axel Hamann** (first call Q3 FY24-25, August 2025). The new CFO's language is more clipped and more willing to concede uncertainty ("cannot be excluded" on impairments; "too early to tell" on HKM), which reads as slightly more candid than the prior "impairments will stop" framing. The terminology around Steel shifted decisively — from "50/50 joint venture" (early 2025) to outright "sale of the majority" to Jindal (late 2025) — a quiet admission that thyssenkrupp wants *out* of steel, not merely to share it. And a new liability surfaced late: the HKM steel joint venture, where thyssenkrupp agreed (February 2026) to let partner Salzgitter take it over, ending slab supply in 2028 — a clean exit, but one requiring provisions.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is a credible, on-schedule breakup of a chronically low-returning conglomerate into separately-valued pieces, run by a team that has proven it can execute a portfolio milestone to the letter even as it chronically over-promises on the operating line.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing:** the value here is a sum-of-the-parts story whose biggest piece — the 51% Marine Systems stake — has *already* been crystallized and re-rated in the open market, and whose next hard catalyst (the Jindal steel sale) has since paused. What remains is real but soft: an announced-but-undated Materials Services separation, a long-dated (antitrust-gated) Elevator payout, and a steel unit whose recent strength is shared-sector policy beta, not company-specific alpha. The parts are worth more than the whole, but much of that gap is now recognized by the market after a ~24% year-to-date run, and the remaining catalysts lack firm dates. Underlying free cash flow is negative and the net-cash cushion is shrinking.

**Moat and terminal value:** the consolidated group has **no durable moat** — negative ROIC, no pricing power in its dominant steel, materials-distribution and auto-components segments, which are commodity, cyclical, low-return businesses. The one genuine franchise (naval defense, a regulatory-license-and-scale moat) is now a separately-listed 51% stake rather than an embedded asset. The structural threat is the energy-transition/decarbonization cost burden on carbon-heavy steel and internal-combustion-linked auto components — real, but currently **cushioned** by EU trade protection and a green-steel investment program, so it reads as manageable rather than terminal. The cheapness is neither a clean fear-print nor a melting base; it is a fairly-priced holding company whose discount narrows only as hard, dated separations land — and the nearest hard one just paused.

# thyssenkrupp AG (TKA.DE) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator pass. Six consecutive quarterly calls, February 2025 through February 2026, cross-referenced against the screener financials. thyssenkrupp is a German industrial conglomerate breaking itself into pieces: it is turning from an operating group into a "financial holding company" that owns separately-listed businesses. Prices in euros; the shares trade on Xetra (ticker TKA).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these six calls is a single, disciplined message repeated until it came true: **"we will break ourselves up, one piece at a time, and let the market pay for each piece separately."** Management calls the framework ACES 2030 and the destination a "lean financial holding company."

At the start of the window (Q1 FY24-25, February 2025) the emphasis was on a *minority* spin-off of the naval-defense business, Marine Systems (TKMS), during calendar 2025, plus a 50/50 steel joint venture with the Czech energy group EPCG. By the middle of the window the steel plan had mutated — first into a collective restructuring agreement with the IG Metall union (May–July 2025), then into a full **sale** of Steel Europe to India's Jindal Steel (disclosed December 2025). By the end of the window (Q1 FY25-26, February 2026) the holding-company vision had hardened into a queue: Marine Systems already spun and listed; Materials Services being "prepared for capital-market readiness"; Automotive Technology re-cut into four units with a non-core piece (Automation Engineering) put up for sale; Steel in due diligence with Jindal.

The one growth driver that was *introduced and amplified* is defense. Marine Systems moved from a footnote to the centerpiece, riding record submarine orders (Germany, Singapore) to a >€16B backlog. The drivers *quietly dropped* were the green-transformation showcases — hydrogen (nucera), carbon capture (Polysius), green steel — which opened most calls in 2025 as proof points and by early 2026 had faded to boilerplate as their end-markets ("hesitant," "project deferrals") disappointed.

**The marquee promise was kept exactly.** Management said it would spin Marine Systems in calendar 2025 at a 1-for-20 ratio, keeping 51% — and on 20 October 2025 it did precisely that, with the stub added to the MDAX mid-cap index within weeks. In a file full of missed top-line forecasts, that delivered promise is the single most important credibility anchor here.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Increasing underlying resilience… EBIT adjusted up despite sales down" (every call) | FY24-25 EBIT adjusted €640M, up €72M year-over-year, on revenue down ~6% to €32.84B. Net income swung positive to €465M (EPS €0.75) from a €1.51B loss. | **True but fragile.** The EBIT-adjusted line genuinely held while sales fell ~€5B over two years. But "adjusted" does heavy lifting — the reported turn to profit leaned on one-offs (an Elevator-stake revaluation of ~€900M in Q4, the Electrical Steel India sale), offset by ~€800M of Steel impairments. |
| "Third consecutive year of positive free cash flow — first time in 20 years" | FY24-25 free cash flow before M&A €363M — but flattered by a >€1B Marine Systems customer prepayment. TTM free cash flow (to 31 March 2026) is **negative €926M**, and FY25-26 is guided **negative** on €700–800M of restructuring cash-out. | **Poorer than the headline.** The streak is real but thin and prepayment-aided; underlying cash generation has already rolled back over. |
| "Impairments at Steel will stop once the new business plan is agreed" (Feb 2025) | Steel impairments recurred every subsequent quarter — ~€100M (Q2), ~€100M (Q3), ~€600M of the ~€800M full-year total (Q4), and further Steel restructuring charges drove a **−€334M** net loss in Q1 FY25-26. Management now says more "cannot be excluded." | **Did not hold up.** This is the clearest broken promise in the file. |
| "Strong balance sheet, net cash ~€4–5B" | Net cash fell from ~€4.3B (Dec 2024) to €3.7B (Jun 2025), rose to ~€5B at fiscal year-end (Sept 2025) on the India sale, then dropped to €3.2B (Dec 2025) and ~€2.7B (Mar 2026) as cash burned. | **True but eroding.** The cash cushion is real, but it is a melting asset while the operating businesses consume cash and restructuring bills come due. Note it also ignores a large pension deficit (~€2.4B in Steel alone). |
| "We keep profit guidance" (repeatedly) | FY24-25 landed inside the (twice-lowered) EBIT-adjusted range of €600M–€1B at €640M; sales guidance was cut three times across the window. | **Half-credible.** Profit guidance was defended and met; the top-line guide was serially walked down. |

The pattern: the *portfolio* claims are trustworthy (they spun Marine Systems on the letter of the plan), the *profit-resilience* claim is real but adjustment-heavy, and the *cash and impairment* claims have consistently flattered a weaker reality.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-rising on portfolio, defensive on operations.** The confidence is bifurcated. On the breakup, management grew *more* specific and assured over time — from "we want to finalize in the course of calendar 2025" (Feb 2025) to a delivered listing and a concrete queue of next names (Feb 2026). On the underlying business, the language stayed relentlessly defensive: "markets don't help," "many industries remain muted," "weak customer demand, particularly in Europe," repeated call after call, with the offense always framed as self-help (restructuring, headcount out, APEX cost program) rather than growth.

A telling late-window shift: by February 2026 management leaned into *external* tailwinds it does not control — a "positive sentiment" in European steel (share prices "up around 50%"), EU import quotas and CBAM (the carbon border tariff), a possible delay to the EU emissions-trading phase-out. That is a subtle move from "we will fix this ourselves" to "the policy environment may rescue the steel unit" — more hopeful, less controllable.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: Medium.** The screener shows a beat rate of just **1 of 6 quarters (17%)** — chronic under-delivery against consensus — and a three-year EPS CAGR of **−25.6%**. Yet management met its own (lowered) EBIT-adjusted guide for FY24-25 and delivered the Marine Systems spin on schedule and to specification. The reconciliation: they sandbag and re-cut the *sales* line, defend the *adjusted-profit* line, and execute *portfolio* milestones on time. What you cannot trust is any forward statement about impairments ("they will stop") or clean cash flow; what you can trust is a dated, structural portfolio commitment once it is formally announced.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts circled the same three sore spots for a year, and management deflected each:
- **How much cash must be injected to separate Steel?** Asked repeatedly (Synagowitz, Q3); answered only with "it will have the required liquidity" and "not ready by year-end." Still unquantified.
- **The net-cash-versus-market-cap gap.** In February 2025, with net cash over €4B against a ~€3B market cap, an analyst put it bluntly: "you could just buy the whole company back." - **What frees up when the government backs Marine Systems?** Management conceded the guarantees "don't have to be backed up by cash" and would not put a euro figure on the financing capacity unlocked.

🟢 **Real, verifiable cost-out:** headcount down ~4,800 in FY24-25, EBIT-adjusted defended while revenue fell ~€5B over two years.
🟢 **Genuine hidden assets crystallizing:** a 16.2% TK Elevator stake, booked ~€2B, now subject to a Kone takeover; separately-listed nucera and Marine Systems stakes.
🔴 **The "last impairment" that never is** — Steel impairments recurred every quarter after being declared over.
🔴 **Cash generation has rolled back over** — TTM free cash flow −€926M; FY25-26 guided negative; net cash down from ~€5B to ~€2.7B in six months.
🔴 **Deep operational weakness** — ROIC −2%, ROE −4.1%, net margin 1.4%, revenue −6% year-over-year, Altman-Z 1.8 (a distress-zone reading); the core is a low-return cyclical.
🔴 **The thesis increasingly leans on policy it does not control** (EU steel tariffs, CBAM, ETS delay).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The CFO turnover is worth noting: Jens Schulte handed off to **Axel Hamann** (first call Q3 FY24-25, August 2025). The new CFO's language is more clipped and more willing to concede uncertainty ("cannot be excluded" on impairments; "too early to tell" on HKM), which reads as slightly more candid than the prior "impairments will stop" framing. The terminology around Steel shifted decisively — from "50/50 joint venture" (early 2025) to outright "sale of the majority" to Jindal (late 2025) — a quiet admission that thyssenkrupp wants *out* of steel, not merely to share it. And a new liability surfaced late: the HKM steel joint venture, where thyssenkrupp agreed (February 2026) to let partner Salzgitter take it over, ending slab supply in 2028 — a clean exit, but one requiring provisions.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** This is a credible, on-schedule breakup of a chronically low-returning conglomerate into separately-valued pieces, run by a team that has proven it can execute a portfolio milestone to the letter even as it chronically over-promises on the operating line.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing:** the value here is a sum-of-the-parts story whose biggest piece — the 51% Marine Systems stake — has *already* been crystallized and re-rated in the open market, and whose next hard catalyst (the Jindal steel sale) has since paused. What remains is real but soft: an announced-but-undated Materials Services separation, a long-dated (antitrust-gated) Elevator payout, and a steel unit whose recent strength is shared-sector policy beta, not company-specific alpha. The parts are worth more than the whole, but much of that gap is now recognized by the market after a ~24% year-to-date run, and the remaining catalysts lack firm dates. Underlying free cash flow is negative and the net-cash cushion is shrinking.

**Moat and terminal value:** the consolidated group has **no durable moat** — negative ROIC, no pricing power in its dominant steel, materials-distribution and auto-components segments, which are commodity, cyclical, low-return businesses. The one genuine franchise (naval defense, a regulatory-license-and-scale moat) is now a separately-listed 51% stake rather than an embedded asset. The structural threat is the energy-transition/decarbonization cost burden on carbon-heavy steel and internal-combustion-linked auto components — real, but currently **cushioned** by EU trade protection and a green-steel investment program, so it reads as manageable rather than terminal. The cheapness is neither a clean fear-print nor a melting base; it is a fairly-priced holding company whose discount narrows only as hard, dated separations land — and the nearest hard one just paused.
